events.excerpt: AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server. This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter. AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs. "Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained. Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity." events.excerpt: The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech. A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered. A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft. In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending. Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers. And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology
events.headline: UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home

events.excerpt: Hi all, I’ve submitted a ZCG grant application and I’m posting it here for community input, as required: Grant Application - PrivateSync: Privacy-Preserving Light Client Sync Infrastructure for Zcash · Issue #549 · ZcashCommunityGrants/zcashcommunitygrants · GitHub The problem: Zashi/Ywallet sync through lightwalletd servers, and that sync leaks the user’s IP address and which compact blocks the wallet downloads — a metadata trail that can deanonymize otherwise shielded activity. lightwalletd’s own wallet-app threat model documents these limitations, and ZCG’s open RFP for lightwalletd infrastructure asks for a multi-operator solution. The proposal: a three-tier privacy stack for light client sync, aligned with upstream work already in flight (librustzcash #2665 , SDK #1741 ): Tier 1 — Tor onion sync for lightwalletd (ships first) Tier 2 — Tor + multi-server PIR, where no single sync node learns which block you requested (information-theoretic, per-server privacy) Deployment: 3–5 independently operated testnet nodes + a runbook so more operators can join — the multi-team model the RFP calls for Ask: $27,000 over 8 months, paid per milestone, no upfront. Evidence base (everything is public): Application repo (proposal, whitepaper, budget, verified research): GitHub - sarinsk629-bl
events.headline: ZCG Application — PrivateSync: Privacy-Preserving Light Client Sync Infrastructure (feedback wanted)

events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it. Voters do see both messages, if they open the proposal and rea
events.headline: One proposal can lift a module's limit and use it in the same block

The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. events.excerpt: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. events.excerpt: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google. On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite. Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications. "An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains. The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip,
events.headline: Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory

events.excerpt: Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G. The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks. At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards. The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic. The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips. The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up. Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G
events.headline: Ye olde server consolidation has made Cisco push top-of-rack switching to 100G

events.excerpt: Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters. That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes. The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts. The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.” Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds. Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194 , and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. events.excerpt: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device. This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes. According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploit

events.excerpt: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult. Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code. "Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model." Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software. Last month, Artcraft , a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5. Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and
events.headline: To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them

events.excerpt: This proposal specifies the JSON document that tokenURI returns in ERC-721 and ERC-6909 and that uri returns in ERC-1155 . Most deployed tokens already use this format, but only part of it was ever specified. ERC-721 and ERC-1155 define name , description and image . Everything else wallets and marketplaces show ( animation_url , attributes and its display_type values, external_url , background_color ) comes from a page OpenSea published in 2018. Clients fill the gaps differently, so the same token renders differently from one app to the next. Draft: erc-8495.md ( ethereum/ERCs#2163 ) The draft covers: Every field and its type, every display_type value in use, and what clients do with values that don’t match, such as booleans, quoted numbers and dates in milliseconds. The URI schemes clients must resolve ( https , ipfs , ar , data ), the ones they may resolve ( ipns , and web3 from ERC-4804 ), and the ones they must never resolve. Fetching rules: ipfs:// URIs instead of gateway URLs, sandboxing HTML in animation_url , and keeping server-side fetches away from private addresses. How later proposals add fields without breaking older clients. events.excerpt: We recommend that all atlantic-2 validators and node operators update to v6.8.0-rc3 . The update is required for RPC nodes. There is no governance proposal and no coordinated chain halt. v6.8.0-rc3 is a release candidate on top of v6.8.0-rc2 . It makes wide eth_getLogs queries cheaper for RPC nodes and stops them early when the client cancels ( #4744 , #4790 , #4791 , #4799 , #4802 ). It also includes the v6.7.4 trace fix, so debug_trace* loads a past block's full validator set ( #4811 ). Wide log queries (over 100 blocks) share a node-wide limit of 30 queries per second. You can now change it with large_log_query_rps under [evm] in app.toml . Set it to 0 to turn the limit off. If the key is missing, the limit stays at 30 ( #4800 ). How to Update Build v6.8.0-rc3 with git fetch --tags && git checkout v6.8.0-rc3 && make install . Stop the node. Replace the seid binary with v6.8.0-rc3 . If you use Cosmovisor, replace the binary in upgrades/v6.8/bin/ . Start the node. Make sure that seid version shows v6.8.0-rc3 and that the node syncs new blocks. events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.headline: Sensors.social: an open air-quality network on Polkadot is growing across the EU

events.excerpt: Summary LlamaRisk proposes to reposition Aave V3 Core as an instance for liquid, bluechip collateral, while the broader range of asset classes is served by Aave V4, where the Risk Premium parameter granularly prices the additional risk each collateral asset carries and more flexible isolation levers exist. The proposal is the next step of the deprecation work, which wound down low-adoption reserves and instances and deprecated the price feeds of long-tail assets . The proposal covers rsETH, osETH, LBTC, tBTC and rETH on Core, together with a group of lower-exposure reserves. As of 9 November 2026 these assets held $1.33B of collateral backing $1.03B of debt. The initial measure is to freeze each reserve in scope, which stops new supply and sets the LTV to zero while leaving existing positions untouched and unaffected. Reserves that are frozen, or frozen by this ARFC, are borrowable, and still carry more than $20k of debt also have their reserve factor raised to 99%. We will then work with each asset issuer and with the largest borrowers on an orderly migration, and allow positions to unwind naturally before taking any further action. events.excerpt: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal
events.headline: Git security vulnerabilities announced
